subtopic: FEDERAL GRANT TO WESTERN VETERINARY COLLEGE

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: FEDERAL GRANT TO WESTERN VETERINARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that I am today writing to the ministers of agriculture for the four western provinces informing them that, subject to the approval by parliament of a vote for the purpose, the government is prepared to make a financial contribution toward the capital cost of constructing and equipping a college of veterinary medicine in western Canada.
The estimate which in due course will be presented to parliament for this purpose will be for a grant of 25 per cent of the cost to a maximum of $625,000. Decision as to the province in which the college will be located will be a matter of arrangement among the western provinces and universities.

subtopic: FEDERAL GRANT TO WESTERN VETERINARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all those who are interested in the agricultural industry in Canada will appreciate the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture. As part of the program of
developing the beef cattle industry it became clear some years ago that there had to be a greater supply of veterinarians in Canada. To that end I had proposed to the four western provinces that they co-operate in the building of this institution and set an example for all similar types of activity in this country whereby co-operation of the various provinces could achieve the end desired by all.
I think the size of the grant proposed by the minister is sensible, because even though the responsibility for education rests with the provinces it is also a fact that the need for veterinarians in the federal service is very great. I think 25 per cent represents approximately the extent to which the federal government should participate. With respect to making a capital grant rather than an operational grant, I think this will probably create a precedent that may prove troublesome in the future, but so far as the statement of the minister is concerned I think the house will generally agree that it is good news.

subtopic: FEDERAL GRANT TO WESTERN VETERINARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group appreciate the announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture, except that we think the federal contribution is rather small in view of the fact that a veterinary college is needed very badly in western Canada. It is recognized and accepted in Canada that the health of animals is a federal responsibility, and we certainly are aware that there is a need for an additional veterinary college to train veterinarians to look after the health of animals. However, when the situation arises where an institution of this nature is being built for the benefit of more than one province, surely this is an area where the federal government should participate rather heavily. While we welcome the announcement that the federal government is finally going to make a tangible offer with respect to building this college, we do not think 25 per cent to a maximum of $625,000 represents the responsibility that the federal government ought to shoulder in this respect.
I believe there is going to be a need for co-operation among the four western provinces in finding the other 75 per cent of the cost of construction and also with regard to the very real consideration of the operating costs after the institution is built. Surely we cannot expect one province to pay for the

Inquiries of the Ministry training of students from other provinces as veterinarians to look after the health of animals. While we welcome this announcement that something is going to be done, we do not feel that 25 per cent represents a fair share of the federal responsibility in this respect.

subtopic: FEDERAL GRANT TO WESTERN VETERINARY COLLEGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture for his announcement that the federal government is prepared to make a grant of 25 per cent of the cost of building a veterinary college in western Canada. There is a crying need in all four western provinces for such a college. The growth of both the livestock and poultry industries has become an important factor in the economy of western Canada, and I think there will be widespread agreement that the minister has done a good thing in agreeing to this grant. I feel certain that the four western provinces will co-operate in seeing that such a veterinary college is constructed.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FINANCING OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FINANCING OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I promised the house
several weeks ago that when I was in a position to do so, I would report on the progress being made at the special assembly of the United Nations regarding the financing of the peace keeping operations of the organization. I am happy to report that the general assembly has now reached agreement on a number of measures concerned with financing of the United Nations peace keeping operations.
The first establishes principles as guide lines for the sharing of the costs of future peace keeping operations. Two resolutions provide for the financing of the United Nations emergency force and ONUC for the last six months of this year. Another appeals to member states to pay up their arrears in respect of their assessed contributions for payment of these operations. Another resolution authorizes the secretary general to continue the sale of United Nations bonds until the end of 1963. A further resolution reestablishes the working group on the examination of administrative and budgetary procedures for the purpose of studying the establishment of a special scale of assessments for financing of future peace keeping operations involving heavy expenditures and of studying the ways and means for reaching a unanimous consensus on questions of
(Mr. Olson.]

principles relating to peace keeping operations in general. The working group is asked to report to the general assembly at its nineteenth session. As the house is aware, Canada is a member of this working group of 21 countries. The seventh and last resolution requests the secretary general to consult all member states and other interested organizations on the desirability and feasibility of establishing a peace fund to receive voluntary contributions from member states as well as from organizations and individuals and to report to the eighteenth session of the assembly.
The Canadian delegation at this special assembly, Mr. Speaker, has played a leading role in the negotiations which led to the adoption of this package of resolutions. I believe that real progress has been achieved at this fourth special session of the general assembly. A solution to the immediate need of the United Nations as regards the peace keeping operations in the Middle East and in the Congo has been found. Further, the general consensus which has emerged in establishing guide lines for the sharing of costs of future peace keeping operations marks an important step in the search for a permanent solution to this problem.
These resolutions, of course, must go to the plenary session, but in view of the large majority which they received in the committee I have no reason to believe that they will fail of adoption. I am sure hon. members will want me to express their thanks to the Canadian delegation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FINANCING OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement which has been made is naturally received with pleasure. However, it does not meet the situation which will culminate on January 1 next. In other words, members of the United Nations refusing to pay their assessments are thereby going to harm this organization. Indeed, if they continue in their course the strength, power and effectiveness of the United Nations as an organization will have been largely emasculated.
What the minister has placed before us is simply a plan for the time being, setting out guide lines as to the courses to be followed. The large issue of the responsibility of member nations in the United Nations to make their contributions and to meet their levies in connection with peace keeping operations, has not been met.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FINANCING OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are pleased to note that this progress has been made as outlined in the report given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Canada has an enviable reputation for carrying her share in the

struggle for peace and in the peaceful development of world resources, both material and human. I am sure our delegation at the United Nations has again proven this fact, and I feel assured that the government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will continue to emphasize the importance which Canada places on making every possible effort for the continuance and improvement of this role of the United Nations.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FINANCING OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is unfortunate that some nations have refused to meet their assessments to permit the logical and proper financing of peace keeping operations in the manner in which it should be carried out. However, I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that, as a makeshift plan, the next best thing is to establish a peace keeping fund. I hope that when such a fund is established Canada will be a substantial contributor to it.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING OF NORTH AMERICAN COMMISSION IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of this question. The North American forestry commission was established in 1959, and held one of its regular biannual meetings in Ottawa last week. It was attended by delegations from the United States, Mexico, and the federal government of Canada; and it is most gratifying that nine of the 10 Canadian provinces were represented at this meeting. awaited with more than ordinary expectation. Everyone tended to believe that the Minister of Finance would reveal that boldness and decision which would justify the slogan "60 days of decision". However, sir, I believe there was never a greater disappointment or sense of betrayal experienced across the country. The mask of arrogance, so well known in the former Liberal administration which was swept from office in 1957, has already become the trademark of this cabinet. Never in my memory has a budget been launched under such a shadow of indiscretion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first observation would be that it has taken approximately 20 minutes of my time to resolve the point of order raised by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). I had not intended to say anything about the business of the house, but his intervention leads me along that way and this might be as good a time as any to say something in that regard. He has failed to expedite the business of this House of Commons satisfactorily and has sought to cover up this failure by the type of tactics he has employed today. The committee structure of the House of Commons is at a standstill in this session, despite the fact we have been in session for some weeks now. The greatest sham ever visited upon this parliament was the setting up of a defence committee, a committee which was set up to silence members of the government party and the sort of questions they were asking in regard to defence matters. Their chagrin was so great on that question that not one single backbencher on the government side spoke on the subject. I think it is fair to say that there was a sullen silence,

particularly from the hon. members from Quebec, when that action was taken in this house.
If I can get down to the budget I should like to say that the action taken last Wednesday was not a responsible one. This was not the type of action one would expect from a minister widely known for his background as an economist, an accountant, and a trader in the investment community of Toronto. There can be only one conclusion: this action was taken without consideration of the consequences in the exchange markets of this country. The reputation of the minister as an expert in bond and stock market activities rules out the conclusion that this was the result of stupidity or ignorance. It is no wonder, sir, that there are many who believe that this was a "pay-off" on a grand scale. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has not helped to subdue this speculation by his outright refusal to recognize the constitutional practice in these matters. If the Prime Minister were really a man who cared he would institute a parliamentary inquiry into this matter with all haste and allow the facts to be established, so that there may be an end to the many varied speculations which are common gossip from one end of this country to the other. Knowing the Secretary of State, who I see is still in the house, as we all know him, as a self-appointed stickler for constitutional procedure and practice, and knowing his experience and knowledge in this regard, there can be no doubt that the action taken last Wednesday was taken deliberately by this government in outright violation of every precedent with which they were familiar. Unrevealed but compelling circumstances must have dictated that action.
The Minister of Finance wants to face the facts. The first fact is that this is not his budget. This is not even the government's budget. This is certainly not the department's budget. This is an outsider's budget. Members of the government have claimed that it took the best brains in Canada to produce this budget. Well, Mr. Speaker, the best brains in Canada laid an egg, and the minister had the painful duty of swallowing that egg last Wednesday. That action on Wednesday was an admission of failure to grasp the task given to the minister by the Prime Minister. I suggest to you, sir, that the best brains to produce a budget are within the government service, among those who have dedicated their lives to protecting ministers of finance and governments from the mistakes that might endanger confidence in the stability and purpose of government in Canada.
This whole matter, Mr. Speaker, also has the earmarks of the Prime Minister, his
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden familiar touch. There is a certain boldness about it, it lacks the carefulness required in matters of great importance to the Canadian people. Indeed, it has not been too much different from the attitude and carelessness which was displayed by the Prime Minister in his announcements last December on the nuclear question. Canadians today have reason to think back to the budgets brought in by the Hon. Donald Fleming, without a doubt the greatest finance minister this country ever had. He was a minister of capacity and vision. His budgets did more for the construction industry and those employed in it than was appreciated at the time. The period when he was minister of finance was marked by the greatest home building program in the entire history of this country. That record will never be matched by this government. The significant achievements of those budgets were widely recognized throughout the world when last year this nation produced the greatest increase in the gross national product of any of the free nations of the world.
The present government, the present Prime Minister and the present Minister of Finance have talked of getting the economy rolling. Why, sir, they cannot even get their budget rolling without creating the biggest scandal that was ever accorded the introduction of a budget in Canadian history. In that process they have contributed more instability and uncertainty in our exchange markets than was ever before experienced. Because of these misdemeanors, some of which seem to have been voluntary and some to have arisen through ignorance, carelessness or arrogance, there would appear to be only one honourable course open to the Minister of Finance. The minister s resignation would go a long way toward restoring confidence in Canada. The Prime Minister has already admitted that this has been the subject of cabinet discussion. There is another course. The Prime Minister might take this budget to the people of Canada and call a general election on this issue. I respectfully submit to you, sir, that the Prime Minister has rejected that course because he is aware that this is hardly an issue upon which he can appeal successfully.
The Minister of Finance wants to face the facts. Well, here are the facts. I have a clipping from that respected and authoritative newspaper the Manitoba Co-Operator which deals with farm income. The clipping indicates that cash incomes to Canadian farmers from farming operations reached an all time high in 1962, 6.6 per cent more than the previous peak total in 1961, and 13.4 per cent greater than the 1960 estimate. I have another clipping from the Bay street Journal which indicates that record breaking incomes have

The Budget-Mr. Nasserden put the farmers in clover. It indicates that total farm net income rose nearly 50 per cent in 1962. Almost every province in Canada showed an increase in their incomes last year from agricultural operations. Another clipping from the Bay street Journal shows that the gross national product reached a six-year peak, and that according to the dominion bureau of statistics Canada had record producton in 1962, which despite a weak fourth quarter climbed 8 per cent to a peak of $40.4 billion. That compared with an increase of 1.6 per cent in 1954.
Here we have one from the Manitoba Co-Operator. The heading is: "Demand for Oats Continues Strong" and the text begins:
Export demand for Canadian oats continues strong compared with previous years-
Next I have a cartoon from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix under the heading: "Farm Income Highest in Canadian History". Here is an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal containing the statement:
President Kennedy estimated today that Canada achieved the best record of price stability among all major industrial countries.
These are the facts, even though hon. gentlemen opposite do not like them. They indicate that the economy of Canada was not only rolling but was actually booming when the present government assumed office last April. I am not apologetic that it took almost four years to get the economy rolling after 22 years of Liberal administration. However, I am concerned when I see a deterioration setting in so soon after their return to power. Look at this headline in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of June 14: "Can't Stop Grain Sales Drop-Sharp". That statement is attributed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). I say to you, sir, and to the Prime Minister that this statement will cost us sales of grain. I say it will have an adverse effect on the price we get for our grain abroad. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has learned nothing from the past when he was so closely associated with a former minister of trade and commerce, the late Mr. C. D. Howe, who is reported to have said; "If they want our grain, let them come and get it". I say to the Prime Minister and to this faceless, careless government that the buoyant position of agriculture during the past few years contributed greatly to the achievement by Canada of the largest increase in the gross national product last year of any of the free nations of the world.
The national program pursued by my leader and encouraged by the Hon. Donald Fleming as minister of finance rescued Canada from the doldrums resulting from Liberal apathy. That national program

brought increasing prosperity to Canadians in almost every community of this nation. Despite this buoyant economy, however, the opposition of those days spread the poison that is fear, particularly in our urban areas. That fear complex still haunts the Liberal party. I say to you, sir, and to the Prime Minister, that a Minister of Trade and Commerce who is caught up with pessimism and fear is a luxury Canada cannot afford.

speechtext:
This government says it wants two ministers of agriculture. This government did not even mention agriculture in the budget. This is what we have come to expect from the present Prime Minister. It is a strange course, considering the pledges which were made during the last campaign. The Prime Minister is a most promising campaigner. I remember him speaking in the maritimes. He promised, there, that if elected his party would do for the maritimes what the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had done for the prairies. When he arrived in western Canada he suggested that if elected he would do for the west what the Leader of the Opposition, as prime minister, had done for the maritimes. He indicated that one of the first acts of a new Liberal government would be to provide $3.00 per bushel for the first 300 bushels delivered by an individual farmer. This was to take the place of the acreage payment.

When I questioned the Prime Minister the other day about his plans in this regard, he was quick to point out that I had not been enthusiastic about that proposal. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have not changed my mind. Furthermore, the failure of this government either to fulfil this pledge or else to honour the commitment we have made is a slap in the face to the grain growers of western Canada.
I should like to remind backbenchers opposite who support the government that their leader made another pledge-a guarantee of $2 per bushel for every bushel delivered to country elevators. I need not say that these were substantial commitments. But this faceless, careless budget has failed to take into account the promises solemnly made by the Prime Minister in western Canada. I ask you, Mr. Speaker: does this look like the action of a Prime Minister who cares?
One of the main objectives of our leader when he was prime minister was to seek an equality of opportunity for all parts of this nation. The maritimes, the prairies and the north were not forgotten in those plans. Central Canada was remembered. We had publicly stated, in all parts of the nation, that attention and effort would have to be directed toward certain problems in the rural areas of central and eastern Canada, with particular reference to the province of Quebec. Our term of office was temporarily interrupted, however, and this budget indicates to me that a tremendous task awaits the next government of this country. Certainly, the present budget does not begin to touch those problems.
I warn the Prime Minister, a budget adding to the burdens of the ordinary people of this country still without homes is hardly what was expected from a Prime Minister who cares. The 11 per cent sales tax is a challenge to the people of this nation. It sets the course to be taken by this administration-a course diametrically opposite that of the government led by my hon. friend from Prince Albert. Throughout the last six years, various building materials were given exemption from sales tax. The home building program of that period was the most successful in Canadian history. More than 750,000 families were able to secure homes under this massive program. That program achieved a level of employment which would not otherwise have been possible. There is still a great need for housing in Canada. I ask the Prime Minister why these people should be asked to make up the tax reductions granted industry in this budget. Is this the way the right hon. gentleman shows he is a Prime Minister who cares?
The Minister of Finance has had more than a thousand telegrams protesting this proposal
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden alone. Most of these are from builders, suppliers and contractors. These people recognize the dangers of this proposal. That is the only answer that can keep our present industrial plant rolling. That is the only answer that will provide additional employment opportunities for Canadians. This faceless, careless budget has forgotten that aspect of our problem altogether.
As I read the budget, it is one of the most faceless, careless documents I have ever examined. If adopted and put into effect it will allow a certain degree of financial juggling that could be expected from stock market experts. The powerful corporations, well established and with healthy reserves and extensive credit, will have a definite advantage over the small businessman trying to become established. Mr. Speaker, I would now like to say a word about the issue of this country's unity, which should be considered as much, if not more, than unemployment or economic depression. The disintegration which has taken place in the last few years in that respect endangers the very life of this country. It was not until the speech made in this house by the present Prime Minister, on December 17 last, that this crucial problem was called to the attention of the whole Canadian people. Since then, an ever-increasing number of Canadians are getting convinced that the time for fundamental choices has come.
In the province of Quebec, there is talk of separatism, of convening the states general, of setting up a federation of almost independent states. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it is not the separatists themselves who are a menace at this time, but those whom I shall call the crypto-separatists. Back in 1911 Laurier warned us, indeed, against those people when he said:
People in the province of Quebec know that there are those who say that this country's business may be settled according to the aspirations of one province; but I tell you that those who dare to maintain such a proposition are nothing but demagogues.
Today's demagogues, Mr. Speaker, like the leader of the Union Nationale and his followers, have become the fellow travellers of separatism. In order to make the headlines and attain popularity, they go one better than the other fellow and set forth proposals which they know cannot be accepted within our federation, without having the courage to tell French speaking Canadians what will happen to them when those proposals are refused.
And it is precisely that masked and hypocritical form of separatism which might lead French Canadians unwittingly to collective suicide. The separatists are not the ones to be


feared but those sorcerers' apprentices of separatism, because in using this movement as an instrument of blackmail, they will provoke a flood which they will soon be unable to control.
Besides the demagogues denounced by Laurier, there are, among English speaking Canadians people who maintain with stubbornness and false pride, that the business of the country can be settled without taking into account the province of Quebec and the indefeasible rights of French Canadians. Without knowing it perhaps, these people are separatists in their own way. Certainly they are fanatics who have not yet understood the real nature of their country.
From the viewpoint of national unity and Canada's future-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I said, on the matter of unity and future for Canada, those English speaking Canadians are just as dangerous as the reactionary capitalists who would be ready to put in jeopardy our economic system rather than go half way in recognizing the right of others.
Personally, as a French Canadian I cannot accept either of those extremes. I would be devoid of any pride if I were to accept the one-way attitude of some English speaking Canadians who behave as if they belonged to a superior race but who fail to cover up their pitiful culture. Besides, for the sake of the most materialistic, and idealistic interests of the French Canadians, I cannot accept separatism even as a piece of bluff, for fear that it may precisely turn against those whom it is supposed to help.

It is on the economic level that separatism would have the most immediate disastrous consequences. It would surely reduce the inflow of foreign capital and would make it more difficult to have access to foreign markets. Those investments and markets are, as we know, absolutely essential not only to ensure the future development of the Quebec economy but also to keep it as it is now. The immediate result of separatism would thus be to reduce substantially the relatively high standard of living to which French Canadians have become accustomed, who surely cannot be compared, in that respect, to economically underdeveloped nations.
The people of French Canada, egged on by irresponsible leaders, might all the same one day accept separatism but they would surely not accept willingly the lower standard of living that would result from it. That sacrifice will have to be imposed on them at the political level. That is why one can conclude that separatism would almost inevitably lead to either a right wing or a left wing dictatorship.
At the cultural level, with our modern means of communications, separatism or more precisely isolation, is impossible. The voice of America would still be heard in Quebec even after separatism. Cultural penetration would continue at a time when the internal sources of culture would be depleted because of economic stagnation and political dictature and would be fatal. Internal differences would inevitably arise and annexation to the United States would soon appear to many as a sort of liberation.
In my opinion, this almost apocalyptic view is not exaggerated. As I see it, economic stagnation, political dictature, cultural depression and annexation to the United States seem the logical results of separatism. This is why French Canadians cannot seriously and quietly consider it as an alternative or even a basis for negotiation; it is at best a solution of despair, a kind of collective suicide.
This is why I believe it is my duty to warn those who play the game of separatism at present, that they may unknowingly be assuming grave responsibilities for those they pretend to be defending. The game is too portentous to inspire bravado at press conferences. It is probably easier and it may even seem more courageous at times to arouse the frustrated feelings of a group rather than 28902-5-99i	.
The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne to use the language of reason in its best interest. But the sorcerers' apprentices of separatism should also have the courage to tell French Canadians that the road on which they are trying to lead them is bound to end up in a blind alley.
The consequences of separatism are unacceptable not only to French Canadians but to all Canadians. On the other hand, coexistence in isolation is no longer acceptable, because French Canadians are left in a permanent condition of inferiority. So, finally, it should be recognized by all of us that a divorce is impossible and that there is only one truly possible solution-a renovation of confederation and, above all, the spirit of confederation.
Confederation was once correctly described as a marriage of reason. It should be added that this is its weakness as well as its strength. Its weakness lies in the fact that it does not foster love. Its strength lies in the fact that it is essential to us because of our economic interests, our need for democracy and freedom and the demands of our cultural survival and development. We, French Canadians particularly, should always remember that confederation in our case remains a beneficient challenge and a factor of unity among ourselves.
But because of its nature, to preserve that marriage, we must use reason, we must negotiate with dignity and pride, without blackmail or stubbornness, being fully conscious that important changes must be made to confederation, but that they cannot be carried out instantly.
The position of this federal government is very clear. We are proposing to all Canadians of good will a new alliance; a confederation that will really be developed in accordance with the principle of equality between the two founding nations, while taking into consideration, of course, the contributions of other cultural groups of more recent origin. All Canadians, either individually or through their representatives, will soon have an opportunity to state their view on that objective and to express their opinion on that serious matter before the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. Somehow, this will be a referendum on the future of our country. I certainly hope that the great majority of Canadians of all walks of life will declare themselves in favour of the proposed general objective, and then it will be possible for the governments, federal as well as provincial, to carry it out in their respective fields.

The Budget-Mr. Lamontagne
As far as the federal administration is concerned, as I said before, we do not want to wait for the commission's recommendations, before taking action.} We want to achieve as soon as possible perfect equality for the two official languages, not only with regard to verbal or written communications with the public, but within every department.'
To that end, various projects are now being considered such as a review of the recruiting and examination system, special courses within the various departments, a premium for bilingualism, the creation of a bilingual institute of public administration, where all university graduates might spend some time before taking up their posts in the federal service.
We shall start with that over-all program next September. From now on, we want all civil servants truly to understand the bilingual and fundamentally bicultural character of Canada. More particularly, we want French Canadians to be able to serve their country in their own language and not to have to forget it when going to work. We also want that transformation to go beyond the civil service; but, to that end, we will need the close co-operation of the provincial governments and of our private cultural institutions. That is why we have to wait for the results and recommendations of the inquiry commission before extending it to other fields.
Another aspect of the present crisis is to be found at the very level of our political structure, our federalism and our federal-provincial relations. We have come to a point where we have to make a fundamental review of our political system. That is not to be wondered at or be afraid of, because federalism is in constant need of reshaping as the role of the government changes and its responsibilities increase. The federal government feels that the time has come to make that review and it is prepared to do it in close co-operation with the provinces. Indeed, it is in that spirit that was established recently a special cabinet committee on federal-provincial relations, which I am privileged to chair.
The Prime Minister announced recently his intention to call a federal-provincial conference next fall. In my opinion this should be but a preliminary meeting aimed, without eliminating the necessity of temporary reviews, at determining the scope of the collective review of our federative regime. Such a conference should be followed by careful

studies of current problems and possible choices; it should also be followed by several other ministerial conferences if we really want to try and rebuild confederation according to the ideals and needs of the Canadian people in our time and of the generations to come. In a word, we must become, as it were, the fathers of a renewed confederation.
We have a little over three years to prepare for the 1967 centenary. In my opinion there is no better way to prepare for such celebration than to collectively wake up our minds about our present identity, and about what we want to become in the future and to collectively take decisions which will be inspired by our consideration of those matters. In such a context, the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism and the ministerial meetings more particularly concerned with our political system will be vitally important.
The task which rests with us during the forthcoming years has a truly historic significance. If we fail, it may be our last opportunity; if we succeed-and I am convinced that we can with good will and foresight- we shall have given a new chance to Canada and to Canadians.

It was held in Jonquiere and I was accompanied by my excellent friend the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote). Thus we had the opportunity to find out anew how beautiful our language is. And no sooner had such a well-filled day come to an end, after much
[Mr. Gregoire.l
praising of the beauty of the French language, than the very next day we are called upon to study a bill like this one in which, if I may put it that way, our beautiful language is spoiled, murdered.

I wonder why a company, from Toronto or elsewhere, or even from Montreal, which wants a French name and asks the parliament of Canada to grant it a French name, does not first secure the services of translation experts who will help it find an appropriate name in French.
Only yesterday, during the celebrations I mentioned earlier, I had the opportunity of realizing the tremendous effort made in the province of Quebec to teach French Canadians to speak their own language better. There was a distribution of prizes, of trophies to young students of our high schools, public schools and convents in the Saguenay and Lake St. John district. Those trophies and prizes were handed to them following competitions in the schools to encourage the students to make a better use of their own French language.
I attended the distribution of prizes and trophies which took place on the occasion of our own annual French Canadian festival. Those trophies were given to those who had written the best French essays and to those who were speaking the best French. If something along those lines is done in our schools, I wonder why we should accept in the House of Commons the kind of French that is suggested to us now.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the hon. member who has introduced this bill to withdraw it of his own accord. and more particularly after witnessing the respect in which the French language is held there, after having heard people praise its beauty and the way it can be used.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, while the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne) waxed eloquent on the comforts of a renovated federalism, his friend -or at least, his ally-Mr. Lesage, premier of the province of Quebec, just happened to have certain statements to make concerning the budget of our Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). I feel sure the Minister without

Portfolio will read with interest, while running through his newspapers tomorrow morning, that Mr. Lesage has described as a violation, and a glaring one-I am told- of provincial jurisdiction the new federal intrusion into fields traditionally reserved to the provincial state.
He attacked especially the financing program proposed by the government for municipalities. At the same time, he took the opportunity to say that the sales tax-proposed by the hon. members opposite-is a backward step. And finally he described as an Indian gift the $500 offered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to encourage building in the winter months.
Now, Mr. Speaker, is that not an example of the take it or leave it attitude, the arrogant attitude of the administration towards the provinces, which are reduced to the status of vassals. And nothing in the remarks of the Minister without Portfolio, this afternoon, indicated that there had been any change of heart in that connection.
It is very nice for the minister to say that with this budget, which has disappointed everyone, we were entering a new era. He said that the budget had enhanced our prestige abroad. He should read Canadian and American papers, such as the New York Times and the New York Herald, and all others to see how many of the budget resolutions have been called discriminatory actions. He said that the budget contains provisions for the recovery of the economy, that those provisions will promote the expansion of our economy, while every building association in this country and every businessmen's association have declared in the strongest possible terms their dismay when faced with those proposals which could entail nothing but a slowing down of economic activity and business and an increase of unemployment.
Finally, the minister said that this budget would lead us into a new phase of national unity and he has called crypto-separatists those who in one way of another would oppose this new concept of federalism the administration was putting before the House of Commons and the population as a whole.
In the light of the statements just made by the premier of Quebec I wonder if tomorrow the minister will not describe him also as a pseudo-separatist.
And as one of the brilliant newspapermen on the hill, Mr. Clement Brown, said in his column: the Minister of Finance is a humor-

ist; on the one hand he proposes measures intended, according to his own words, to strengthen confederation but, on the other hand, he intrudes violently into the very substance of the confederation pact.
I do hope that before long we shall have the opportunity to discuss those measures in greater detail and the violation of the provincial autonomy which they revealed.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I will continue my remarks in English. I wish to state that the country as a whole was looking forward with great anticipation to this first budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). That was to be the crowning achievement of the 60 days of decision, the 60 days of action. That was to be the great piece de resistance of that period which, incidentally, the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) in a radio address the other day declared could not be compared with any other period in modern history. Well, that is going quite a long way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, that is very true: it certainly cannot be compared with any other period of political history in Canada, because we have had the days of inaction and the days of consideration-qualified inaction- and I have made a summary and calculated a balance sheet. In 60 days of "action" I have found that the principal achievement of the government has been its unequalled ability to consider matters placed before it for attention. Looking through reports in Hansard from May 12 to the end of the period of decision, I find that the government had no less than 56 matters which, they told this house, they had taken under consideration- I may have left out one or two. They had, in addition, 21 matters under review. They also had 24 matters under study. One might say the government was engaging in generalities by saying these matters were under review or under study. But there is a fine distinction. Among other things, the government has certain matters under active consideration. No less than six questions, we are told, were under active consideration. Some were under serious consideration, and still others were under very serious consideration. With regard to matters taken under review, we have been told that the government is taking a look at some of these questions. Other questions were kept under constant review. Still others were being watched very closely. Certain subjects, we were told were being given close study. As a matter of fact, some were currently under study and others were being studied with great attention. I do not even refer to those matters which are under continuous study, or constant review, or to
The Budget-Mr. Martineau which close consideration is being given. Of course, there are other matters which are not being considered at all; they are not even worth consideration.
But there is no doubt that the crowning achievement, the budget was an anticlimax. It was a flop. It simply signified the floundering of the financial proposals announced with so much pomp, so much flourish. The budget itself could hardly have justified the sactimonious and partisan introduction made by the minister. It seems to me that everybody is out of step except the hon. gentleman himself. Consider the arrogance shown by the minister in some of his introductory passages. Nevertheless, the minister could defy his horoscope on that famous night of June 13. He was not superstitious. He was going to give the nation the great "face the facts" budget. He and his colleagues were taking this budget very seriously. It was to be an occasion announcing a grand scrutiny of the state of affairs confronting this nation. He was going to present to parliament an account long overdue. Here, the minister took on the role of a public indicator-a sort of public prosecutor or grand inquisitor-and he discussed with flippancy the progress of the economy. This is what he said about 1962, one of the years in which our economy achieved remarkable, indeed, unprecedented progress. He said:
The year 1962 was a remarkable one in Canadian economic history. It was marked by an exchange crisis which followed upon five years of economic stagnation.
He had not one word to say about the remarkable success of the emergency measures, or of the restoration of our reserves to a new high. Nevertheless, he did have to admit that 1962 was a good year. This is what he said:
The year 1962 . . . was an improvement over 1961. This was evident in the industrial part of our economy, while in agriculture, too, incomes were up.
The details he said, could be found in the white paper. In other words, these solid achievements were referred to as something worth only the attention of scholars or people who wanted to delve more deeply into the history of this nation. His sense of balance had been disturbed. The minister said the previous government had permitted the economy to stagnate, but he himself predicted a rate of growth much smaller than last year. He said, as will be found reported at page 1002 of Hansard:
We have built our present estimate of revenues on the assumption that our gross national product will be about 5 per cent greater in 1963 than it was in the previous year. For this purpose we have assumed a normal crop, a relatively stable price level from now on. and no external trouble. About one third of this 5 per cent represents price increases-

The Budget-Mr. Martineau
The minister referred to confidence. Confidence, he said was a state of mind. It was psychological in character. The minister charged that the previous administration had destroyed confidence. He also said that as a result of the election and the prospect of a decisive government in Canada once again, Canada is on the road up.
Well, I wonder if the minister has read any of the newspapers in this land lately. This is a budget which can be criticized both because of its form and because of its substance. In regard to its form, I can only say that this is a matter which has been discussed in great detail during the last few days. I do not wish to go further into this aspect of the controversy. The fact remains that there has been a serious violation of constitutional practice in comprising the security of a budget by the way in which the minister permitted his special advisers access to the final draft. He can say all he likes about its being a good thing to have advisers, but there is surely no justification whatever for giving advisers brought in from outside access to the final draft of the budget. It remains a fact that it is not necessary only for Caesar's wife to be above evil; it is necessary for Caesar's wife to be above the suspicion of evil. That is the point which we on this side have tried to bring out, without attacking in any way the integrity of the minister or his aids. We have not attempted to do this in any way but we have discharged what we believe to be our parliamentary duty by placing before this house and the nation the extraordinary practices which have prevailed, extraordinary, surely, in Canadian political history, surrounding the presentation of the budget. Yesterday, the minister failed to give an answer to that charge. It is all right for him to say that he may have made a mistake and that he is sorry for having made a mistake. But this does not preclude the fact that there has been indiscretion and that the civil service has been flouted. Even yesterday in making his excuses to the house the minister said he had disregarded the old, traditional, safe and cautious way of proceeding, and was innovating. If he has innovated, he has innovated to the detriment of the confidence which should reign in these matters not only in parliamentary circles but throughout the nation.
With regard to the contents of the budget itself, Mr. Speaker, I would say that it is a sort of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde budget. It has an air of unreality. I think one can say that one is travelling in Alice's wonderland and that the minister has taken an attitude somewhat like Humpty Dumpty in the attitude of impenetrability he has assumed. That is so, Mr. Speaker, because the minister, after having stated objectives with which

none of us could disagree, proposed means that will have the effect of defeating these very objectives. That is true with regard to his objective of economic expansion. He said we have to get the economy rolling again, we have to cure unemployment, we have to cure the balance of payments problem and the deficit problem. The methods which he employs, Mr. Speaker, defeat these very worth-while and laudable objectives.
Yesterday the minister said there were only a few ways by which to obtain these objectives. They were by imposing one of three taxes, an increase in personal income and corporation taxes, an across the board increase in the sales tax or the removal of the exemption from sales tax of building materials and production machinery. I seem to remember that when the minister was on this side of the house he always spoke of more revolutionary and more novel methods. Expansion was his byword. Where is that expansion today? Shall we find expansion in the imposition of an 11 per cent sales tax on building materials?
With regard to the imposition of that tax the minister said that it was not a very unpopular tax and in fact would be greeted quite favourably by most people in this country. I wonder whether the howl of protest that greeted the imposition of this tax will be looked upon by the minister as indicating a favourable outlook toward the prospect of this tax, which will have as one of its results an increase in the cost of building. Another more serious result is that many worth-while projects will be discarded.
The minister talked about foreign ownership in our country and this is what he had to say about foreign ownership and control, as found on page 1000 of Hansard for June 13:
We shall continue to need substantial net inflows of foreign capital for quite a few years to come if we are to avoid further exchange rate difficulties and if a reasonable increase in our standard of living is to be achieved. This is a fact of life in Canada. It would be the height of folly to ignore it.
Then he quoted Walter Lippmann, apparently with approval, as follows:
The solution of the problem is not one for legislation or treaty but for voluntary action by the United States interests in co-operation with their Canadian associates.
What the minister has proposed, Mr. Speaker, is not voluntary action by United States investors and Canadian investors but rather penalties imposed on foreign investors, on people whom the minister recognizes we need to develop and expand our economy. Yet here he is shaking a big stick at these people and discouraging investments that we need.

On the other hand, we do not offer the proper incentive for the formation of Canadian capital. There is nothing in this budget that will favour greater Canadian participation and that will make a greater amount of funds available for investment in Canada by-Canadians. The budget provides only added taxation and absolutely none of the incentives whereby Canadians can feel that industry will reap the reward which will permit the building up of an intrinsically Canadian industry and which will eliminate part of the foreign ownership and control that all of us in this house deplore.
All of us agree with the objectives that the minister is seeking to achieve, but I think that the business community and businessmen throughout the country are unanimous in stating that the methods employed by the minister go contrary to the end which he seeks. The same administrative difficulties that prevailed in the case of the securities takeover tax, which has been repealed by the minister, are also prevalent in the imposition of the withholding taxes. The same reasons apply to the withholding taxes as applied to the securities takeover tax, and for that reason I submit that the minister should again review this tax, with that constant attention which his colleagues have given to other problems, and repeal it before it is too late.
I have presented in summary form my views with regard to some of the principal points contained in the budget. We will have occasion to come back to them during the discussion of the budget resolutions. A survey of the press throughout the land indicates that the budget is a most disappointing one. That was the first impression that most observers got after the delivery of the budget speech, and after a careful and more lucid analysis of the details of the budget this disappointing budget has become a really disastrous budget. It is disastrous for the expansion of our economy. It is disastrous because its net result will be more unemployment, not less. Its net result will be the discouragement of incentive enterprise and initiative in this country. It is not at all the type of budget the country was expecting from the new administration and from the Minister of Finance who was supposed to bring to bear a wholly novel outlook on financial matters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make some observations in connection with the budget and the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) a few days ago I have an urge to give in a few words my conception of what a budget address should be. I have had the privilege of listening to many budget speeches and it has always been my opinion that a budget speech presented an account to parliament or to a legislature of the state of the nation. Then after giving a statement of conditions as they were, both financial and economic, the gentleman delivering the budget speech, whatever his official position might be, would give a review of the measures which the government proposed to take to meet existing problems and improve conditions. I have gathered the impression, from some degree of experience, that extraneous remarks of a partisan nature are out of place in a budget speech; that generally speaking ministers making budget speeches deliver them in a noble state of mind and, shall I say, with a noble attitude toward the report and the people listening to the report. The minister, apparently, in delivering his budget speech had no such idea. Whether he got other plans from some of these newly found advisers, I am in no position to say, but nevertheless his speech has been described as the most petty, picayune, partisan party address that has ever been given in parliament. It has been described as a combination of partisanship and platitudes, without being sure which was the more prevalent. To me it indicates supreme arrogance.
The minister called it a face the facts budget. I say that in the light of subsequent events the only face there is in it is an about face, and it now should be called the off again, gone again, will it be on again budget. I strongly advise the minister to go back to writing books. When he chose the title for his book "Troubled Canada" he must have been looking into a crystal ball and seeing the conditions existing in June, 1963 after he delivered the budget speech, because he has certainly added to our troubles by the provisions of his first budget.
25, 1963
The Budget-Hon. H. J. Flemming
I am not one of those who blame the minister entirely for the situation that exists; neither do I find fault with him exclusively. My experience has been that ministers of finance and ministers generally speaking do not take distinct and unusual steps without consulting the prime minister under whom they serve, and other members of the government. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not blaming the Minister of Finance entirely for the situation in which we find ourselves in connection with various things which I will enumerate in a moment or two. Over the years the Minister of Finance has proved himself to be a good theorist. He was good enough to play his part in fooling the electorate last April. His first opportunity to put his economic theories into practice, however, has been a tragic failure and the theories just do not work.
As an example let us consider the 30 per cent tax on sales to non-residents of stock in Canadian companies exceeding $50,000 a day by one seller, which took effect as he spoke the words. How did it work? In a few days it wrought such havoc that Mr. Kierans, the president of the Montreal stock exchange, strong Liberal that he is, forsook his desk and rushed to Ottawa to join forces with Senator Gelinas, who is a collector of funds for the Liberal party, to insist upon the immediate withdrawal of this dangerous tax which was an affront to business at home, in Washington and elsewhere. These gentlemen got results; the tax has been withdrawn and its future is nebulous. The minister, as I say, called his budget a face the facts budget. I repeat that it is an about face, an off again, gone again, when will it be on again budget. As far as I know it is the first of its kind in Canadian political history. Before the election the Liberals talked about restoring confidence; since the election they have acted in such a way as to throw the whole business community of Canada into confusion. How is anyone doing business or contemplating making an investment in this country to know where he stands? How is anyone to know what the tax policy of this about face government is or is not?
I find myself constrained to offer some comments regarding our economic relations with other countries, especially with the United States of America. I am a Canadian. I have many friends and relatives in our neighbour country to the south. I represent a constituency lying along the border of the state of Maine. I have an American-born daughter-in-law living in Canada and contributing to raising young Canadians. All my life I have been associated with businesses which export the bulk of their products to the U.S.A. Moreover, it was American capital

The Budget-Hon. H. J. Flemming which in many instances kept our businesses going by making advances when we could not borrow the money in Canada. Do you wonder, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot get very excited or exercised unduly when I hear about our friends in the United States buying Canadian businesses. I think we might all remember that they do not move the plant and machinery out of this country when they purchase it. The activity remains here. The business employs Canadians. The business pays them well. The business operation is subject to Canadian laws.
The Liberals in the last two elections unfortunately managed to convince Canadians in some localities that we the Conservatives, were anti-American. Speaking for myself, and I think for my party, nothing could be further from the truth. That was not and is not a fact, and it is too bad that many people were influenced by this misrepresentation.
The minister said in his speech that in seeking solutions to this problem, meaning unemployment, our salvation does not lie in isolationism; that it does not lie in withdrawing unto ourselves and ignoring the currents of progress and change around us. I wonder what he was doing with the 30 per cent tax, having uttered those particular words? I believe it is a great privilege for us in Canada to live alongside a wonderful country with such wonderful people as those who live in the United States of America. I think it should be considered as being of great benefit to us and that we should take advantage of our geographical situation instead of whining about it. That is, as long as our laws are respected.
I submit that it is a good thing to have people from other countries thinking that Canada is a good country in which to invest. What is wrong with it? I submit that investment from abroad stimulates interest in this country, or any other country. After investing in Canada people come to visit us. They want to see their security. Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, the account in the book "David Harum" about the country banker, who said that a man's heart is located much closer to his breeches pocket than to his breast pocket? Then we also have from Holy Writ the assertion that "where your treasure is there will your heart be also". So I do not view with alarm the matter of U.S. investment in Canada; in fact, I welcome it.
The 30 per cent tax was ill conceived, ill-prepared and ill considered; it has now been withdrawn. It was too hot to handle and the government had to drop it. I suggest to the Minister of Finance, or whoever he may be in future, that the problem of dividends from Canadian business in their relation to our


balance of payments position should be a matter to be dealt with from the positive point of view rather than the negative. I think it should be made attractive for Canadian citizens to own Canadian stocks rather than apply any extraordinary penalty to foreign owners. This could be accomplished by increasing the discount allowance for income tax purposes on dividends of Canadian companies by a small percentage each year until a certain maximum is reached. It is now 20 per cent. It might be increased by 1 per cent each year over a ten year period, and in that length of time it seems to me that Canadians would bid for stocks of Canadian companies and the ownership in Canada should, and perhaps would, increase enormously.
My opinion, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the sad situation in which the new budget has plunged us is this. In control of our affairs in this house today we have a group of men, most of whom have lived very sheltered lives. They have never had any practical experience in running business. Instead of having to scratch around to earn a living for themselves, generally speaking all they have had to do is to put their names on the back of a regular pay cheque. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that such men have nothing in their background to enable them-

and I include the minister, because he is one-can talk convincingly about how to run the country, but already their actions speak louder than words and prove their incompetence. I say to them, Mr. Speaker, that the best education in the world is secured by struggling to make a living.
I should like to comment on the bringing in of these so-called experts from outside to advise the minister as to what he should put in his budget. I feel that this casts doubts on the abilities of the Prime Minister, of the members of his cabinet, on all Liberal members in this house, and on the fine senior civil

servants whose professional training and personal competence must surely have prepared them to give just such advice at just such a time.
You will recall that only a few years ago a minister of finance resigned in Britain because of a supposed leak before his budget was presented to the house. I feel very strongly that we should hesitate a long time before we break away from practices that have proved themselves through the centuries in the experience of the mother of parliaments; in that-
Land of settled government,
That land of just and old renown,
Where freedom broadens slowly down From precedent to precedent.
The Minister of Finance, like all members of the house, was elected by the people and is responsible to the people. They elected him because they believed he was competent to carry on their affairs. If he felt he was not capable, in consultation with the usual persons whose advice is permissible through parliamentary precedent, then he should never have accepted the position of minister of finance. In my opinion he has made a grave mistake in introducing into this house a very wrong, unfair and dangerous precedent. Some people say: Well, you have to have advice. I see nothing wrong with seeking advice, but the point is that the people from whom the government or the minister secures advice should not know what is going into the budget. They should be asked for advice but they should not know what the decision is. That is the fact, Mr. Speaker, and it is the fault I find with this situation.
Now I have a word or two to say about unemployment. There is no difference between any two members in this chamber as to the importance of unemployment and the tragedy which the lack of gainful work brings to individuals, to families and to communities. That is one of the things we can agree on for sure. Now let us find out how the minister proposes to deal with it in his budget speech. We know of the displacement of people due to automation. We know of the necessity of training people for jobs requiring skill, and the government which preceded the present government took no back seat from any other government in the things they did in that respect. The Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) says that these measures will be expanded. We all know this will take time. What are we going to do in the meantime? What are we going to do for jobs while this training process is going on? That is the question. I can tell hon. members that the industry which employs the largest percentage of unskilled labour in

The Budget-Hon. H. J. Flemming Canada is the construction industry. This includes the forest products industry which produces lumber used for most types of building. I believe the percentage of wages paid in the lumber and construction industry in relation to the total cost of the product compares very favourably with the similar percentage in any other industry. A good deal of the cost of the product is paid to unskilled workers. I have in my hand a letter which was sent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) by the maritime lumber bureau. I commend this to the attention of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Nicholson) also, because this is a protest against the imposition of the 11 per cent tax. I intend to read the letter. This was sent to the Minister of Finance on June 20 and it says:
The directors of the maritime lumber bureau strongly protest the sales tax that has recently been placed on lumber and building supplies.
Increased cost of domestic lumber, by taxation, will result only in less building starts, and have adverse effects on employment in lumber, construction and transport industry.
The loss of the exemption, available to producers and manufacturers on equipment and supplies used directly in the manufacture of lumber, can only result in substantially higher cost and thus weaken our position to compete in our much needed export market. The export market has been built up and maintained over a period of many years and is the basic market for Canadian lumber.
Furthermore, the increased cost of fuel used in the production of lumber, due to the sales tax, is also a serious matter and substantial cost, as a large percentage of our maritime mills are powered with diesel engines.
It is our opinion that the lumber industry of the maritime provinces, presently struggling for existence, is in the position that if such burdens are imposed we will fall into the class of industries that require substantial government assistance in order to exist and compete in foreign markets.
So I appeal again to the minister to reconsider the imposition of this iniquitous 11 per cent tax. This is an industry which should be encouraged. I go back to the question of the training of young men for skilled jobs. It does not make sense that during the period of education and transition we should discourage industries which are using a high percentage of unskilled workers. But what do we find? I will tell you what we were told in the budget speech. We were told that this industry would be encouraged by being taxed 11 per cent on all materials used for construction, which, it is estimated will increase the price of finished units by 5 per cent or more. Could anything be more stupid than that? If ever there was a move that is bound to slow down the construction industry on which so many of our people depend for a living, it is certainly the withdrawal of the sales tax exemption on building materials and the imposition of the manufacturers 11 per cent sales tax on these construction

The Budget-Hon. H. J. Flemming essentials. The sales tax newly imposed on machinery used in manufacturing or production other than farming and fishing is also bound to be a deterrent to the good times we enjoyed in 1962, the best year in the economic history of Canada, thanks to the practical policies of the Diefenbaker government.
The minister, speaking for the government, states that any Canadian, young or old, who wants a job must be able to find one. With that, I agree. Then, almost before the words have left his lips, he imposes a tax of 11 per per cent on all building materials, which will have the effect, if proceeded with, of hindering, hampering and, in many cases, completely stopping work which employs more unskilled men than most other industries in Canada.
I wonder if the minister has read an extract from the newspapers about the Bathurst Power and Paper Company Limited. I wonder if he knows what they are doing with regard to the board mill they were going to build in the Gaspe peninsula. This is from the Moncton Transcript of June 22:
R. A. Irwin, president of Bathurst Power and Paper Co. Ltd. said Friday night the company has decided to reconsider plans for construction of a new kraft board mill in Quebec's Gaspe peninsula.
He said in a telephone interview the review was deemed necessary in the light of the federal government's budget proposal for removing the exemption of building products and machinery from the 11 per cent sales tax.
"This would have a direct effect on the capital cost of the mill", said Mr. Irwin.
Cost was originally anticipated at between $40 million and $42 million. Mr. Irwin said removal of the exemption could increase the figure by an estimated $2,500,000 to $3 million.
I submit that this has every appearance of being the essence, indeed the quintessence of stupidity, and I appeal to the government to remove this tax before it does irreparable damage.
And this is not all. The minister then proceeds to impose a tax on machinery which also will have the effect of cancelling, or at best postponing, the expansion of industry during the period when we need all wheels turning to meet the need for employment and when it would appear desirable to instal machinery and keep it going.
Now I turn to winter employment. The minister mentioned the announcement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) on this subject. The Minister of Labour has stated that $500 will be allowed off the basic price for houses substantially constructed during the winter season. As my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) said a few evenings ago, this is more than offset by the extra tax on building materials. So the Minister of Labour giveth and the Minister of Finance taketh away. I know there is something more

to it than that, but I do not know who is to be called blessed. It is estimated, I believe that 50 per cent or more of the cost of a house is for materials which go into it. In other words, substantially more than the $500 goes for the extra taxes and, actually, the cost of winter construction is substantially greater than if made during more moderate weather. On balance the tax must be considered as additional cost and as taxation. Increasing taxation in itself is bad enough, but applying taxation to the extent of reducing its volume to an industry on which the government depends for an improvement in the employment situation, seems inept and inane and capable of being represented as insane.
The Liberals are attempting to say they have achieved a budget which does not increase taxes, although how this is possible when the minister expects to receive $170 million more in revenue is far too subtle for a mind like mine. They call taxation revenue and expect the people to swallow that in the same way as they did some of their claptrap last April.
I come now to a question regarding the Canada development corporation. What is the intent of this?

speechtext:
Today I should like to discuss some of the aims and implications of the budget recently presented. The purposes of the budget, as clearly indicated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), are fourfold. The first and most important aim is to fight unemployment. The second is to encourage Canadian participation in the ownership and control of companies operating in Canada. The third aim is to make our tax system more fair and equitable by closing loopholes and eliminating anomalies in our taxing statutes. The fourth aim is to move this country toward financial responsibility by reducing the huge budgetary deficits which have plagued us during the past several years. I believe that new ground has been broken in this budget. Bold new ideas have been introduced which, in the years to come, will benefit every part of this country.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the matter of attacking chronic unemployment which all of us, I am sure, consider to be Canada's major problem. Governments cannot tackle this problem alone but they can create an environment in which free enterprise can move forward, and I believe that, working together, labour, industry and government can achieve much in returning this country to a state of full employment.
One of the chief problems we have in Canada is the fact that some areas in our country have not developed as rapidly as others and therefore suffer more from unemployment than does the country as a whole. The Minister of Finance offers in this budget particular encouragement for such areas by saying that new manufacturing and processing industries locating there, regardless of ownership, will have a tax holiday of three years. In addition, they will have the opportunity to write off their machinery and

The Budget-Mr. Benson equipment in a two year period. New buildings for commercial or industrial purposes in these areas may be written off over a five year period.
I believe that these are real incentives to industry. They tell manufacturers and processors that they can move into these areas and have real tax advantages. A manufacturer can set up a new business with the knowledge that if it is economically sound- and no one will start a business anywhere unless there is reasonable hope of its being profitable-he can recover his whole investment before he has to pay any income taxes. These incentives are greater than have ever been offered before in this country to my knowledge. They are incentives designed to encourage industrial growth and expansion in areas of Canada which need it. In addition, for all areas of Canada manufacturing and processing businesses owned to the extent of 25 per cent by Canadians are to be allowed to write off their new machinery and equipment in two years.
I have prepared a table which shows that a manufacturer who is operating profitably anywhere in Canada will be better from a cash flow point of view in spite of the sales tax on building materials, and I would appreciate having the opportunity to insert this table in Hansard at this point with the consent of the house.
