In this table I have assumed that a new manufacturer, with at least 25 per cent Canadian ownership, builds a plant anywhere in Canada and invests $300,000 in buildings and $300,000 in equipment. This table indicates, Mr. Speaker, that over the two year period his depreciation which could be claimed for income tax purposes would, in the two years after budget date, amount to $347,467 as compared with $137,250 at ordinary rates. The extra depreciation would amount to $210,217 and the tax thereon at the corporate rate of 50 per cent would mean a saving of $105,108.50. Thus, Mr. Speaker, even though the manufacturer had to lay out an additional $48,000 when he bought his plant due to the sales tax increase, if he operated profitably he would be $57,108.50 better off from a cash flow point of view after two years of operation than he was before the budget. When businessmen enter a new business, Mr. Speaker, one of their prime concerns is how soon they can get their investment back out of the business and into their hands for further use.
There are other measures, Mr. Speaker, in the budget such as the special payment to employers of elderly workers, the reduction of N.H.A. interest rates and the lower down payment on N.H.A. homes, all designed to spur employment. I believe that these measures, plus other measures such as increased municipal aid, additional retraining assistance, the creation of a department of industry and a national economic council will provide a comprehensive attack on the unemployment problem that we have in this country, a problem which this government is determined to solve.
I should like to move on to the next aim of this budget, namely the encouragement of

Canadian participation in ownership and control of corporations operating in this country. Several members of the opposition have said that they agree with this aim, and then wandered off to discuss the 30 per cent takeover tax, a tax which formed only a minor part of this program and which has since been withdrawn.
We have still in this budget, Mr. Speaker, two major incentives to encourage the sale of a portion of the capital stock of such corporations to Canadians. These are, first, the differential in withholding tax and, second, the accelerated depreciation which I have just discussed. Both of these measures will encourage these companies to sell at least 25 per cent of their shares to Canadians, and to have 25 per cent of their board of directors made up of Canadian citizens who are not company employees. This is new ground which this government has broken. It is the first time that a Canadian government has faced up to the problem of foreign control and ownership. It will mean that Canadians will have a voice in the policies of companies which are operating in Canada, using Canadian resources and manpower, and that we, as Canadians, will be able to share in the profits of such corporations.
I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, about measures which have been included in this budget to close loopholes and eliminate anomalies in our taxing statutes. For several years now there have been a number of loopholes in our taxing statutes which permitted taxpayers who could afford competent advice to escape paying their fair share of taxes. This was accomplished through dividend stripping, corporate income splitting, the misuse of lease option agreements, and the use of the corporate structures of companies which had accumulated losses and were out of business. We will have an opportunity of dealing with these matters in more detail during discussion of the resolutions and bills.
In this budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has proposed drastic steps to plug these loopholes. The purpose of these steps is to help the ordinary taxpayer in Canada by assuring that all taxpayers will pay their fair share of the cost of government.
This could have been accomplished, Mr. Speaker, by taking a year or so to amend the Income Tax Act, which has become extremely complicated over the past several years. However, in the move to equity and fair play, it was essential that action be taken at once. This action has been proposed in the budget, and in two cases it involved the use of a ministerial discretion. I have learned in the past few days, Mr. Speaker, as a result of listening to the discussions in this house, that

The Minister of Finance stated yesterday that the suggestion of many people that we assure the right of appeal from this discretionary power would be considered, and considered it will be, Mr. Speaker. However, as Canadians, I believe that it is the first duty of all of us to see that these abuses are stopped. I say this in spite of the many protests we will receive from persons who have a pecuniary interest in seeing these practices continued.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in closing I should like to say a few words about the removal of the sales tax exemption on building materials and production machinery. As the Minister of Finance mentioned yesterday, the imposition of additional taxes is never popular. However, the idea has been spread that the construction industry is being penalized. This is not the case. The sales tax presently applies to almost everything except food. Clothing, household appliances, furniture and automobiles, to mention but a few of the necessities of life, are and have been for many years subject to sales tax in this country.
It has been stated also in this house that the cost of housing is going to soar. This is also not the case. The best estimate which I have been able to obtain indicates that the selling price of homes at the $10,000 level will increase by about 34 per cent, whereas the selling price of homes in the $17,000 range will increase in price by about 44 per cent. I have calculated the down payment and monthly payments for homes purchased under N.H.A. before and after the revised down payment and interest rates proposed by the Minister of Finance in the budget.
Let us consider a home which previously sold for $13,000 and which may now be increased in price to $13,500. Before the budget, the down payment on this house would have been $900. After the budget, the down payment is $800. The monthly payment prior to this budget would have been $82.67, and it will now be $84.82. Thus, Mr. Speaker, the immediate cash outlay at time of purchase will be $100 less and the monthly payments over 25 years will be increased by $2.15 per month. I do not believe this indicates the catastrophic effect on the small homeowner which has been indicated by some hon. members opposite.
Yesterday in this house, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) presented a statement indicating some of the matters presently in the Excise Tax Act and the budget resolutions. Last evening the hon member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) indicated

The Budget-Mr. Marcoux that this was at variance with the legislation and the budget resolutions. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement simply outlined the position as it exists and I was rather surprised that the hon. member for Perth, himself a chartered accountant, was not aware that the exemptions indicated by the minister were written into the statute many years ago and have not been changed in any way through the budget resolutions.
Finally, I should like to say that in my opinion this is a good budget. It is a bold budget and it is a budget which faces up to tackling some of Canada's basic problems.
I am sure that other measures will be taken towards the avowed aims of this budget and, Mr. Speaker, I believe they will be taken by this government, which is determined to solve these serious problems.

Mr. Speaker, the events surrounding the budget speech have gravely shaken the structures which make for good life in this country of ours.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), in the partisan innuendos of his budget speech, clearly charged the Conservative government of deteriorating the confidence of England and the United States in Canada.
The fact that a tax was imposed and then withdrawn on the purchase of Canadian stocks by foreigners has certainly not enabled the Liberal party to regain that confidence Canada had lost.
As a matter of fact, this has only contributed to aggravating the strong feeling of insecurity across the country. It is also apparent that Canadians have less and less confidence in the future of our country, our institutions and themselves.
People are becoming aware that neither the government nor leaders in other fields have been able to assess the actual problems of the day and to try to solve them. On the other hand, you see all sorts of slightly cracked individuals get front page coverage in the papers, top billing on radio and television, to offer us incredible universal remedies; these self-appointed oracles should rather rank among "fools on the market place".
Undoubtedly, most of the hon. members are under the impression that Social Credit is simply a money and credit theory. This is a serious mistake, for Social Credit is much more than that; it is a philosophy of life based on the respect of man and his freedom of enterprise, two things tending to disappear from our country at the present time.

And, Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that Social Credit is not just a theory. And even if its theories can only be implemented in part, Social Credit philosophy is the basis of the two best provincial governments we have at the moment, that of British Columbia and that of Alberta. And the overwhelming victory scored recently by the Manning administration in the latter province abundantly supports this fact.
And outside those two areas, the sixties have been characterized by a lack of philosophy and intellectual confusion among the leaders, in the political field as well as in others.
The people feel that insecurity and they are concerned; it is time our political leaders realized it.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a few examples. On April 19, 1961, speaking in Sarnia, the then prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, said that the nations should get together in order to produce a philosophy they could support. Unfortunately, he was unable to find a formula that would hold its own against communism. Even the leader of the opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, whose reputation is so well founded in the field of international affairs, did not see fit to take up the challenge. Even less the loudmouths who have a solution to every problem under the sun.
What happened? Has communism disappeared? Has it ceased being a threat? In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the communist threat is greater and nearer than in 1961 and yet I challenge you to find a political leader, apart from the leader of the Social Credit party, who has made one sensible speech on communism during all that time.
And, Mr. Speaker, what leadership has the present government given on this problem as on many others? The people of Canada are surely aware of that because, in three elections under the leadership of the present Prime Minister, the Liberal party has failed to show them on what principles its program was based.
In my own province, we have had a few elections these past years and there has been a complete change of government. The Union Nationale party, after dominating the people at will during almost 20 years, was defeated. And one of the main factors which led to this change is not without importance. Two clergymen wrote a philosophical treatise to the effect that public and political morals were in contradiction with Christian philosophy.

There is no doubt that this forceful publication has decided the people to give to the provincial Liberal party a mandate to govern according to the principles of Christian philosophy. Unfortunately, the Liberal party soon forgot this and the two clergymen have taken another direction.
It is obvious that the people in Quebec were right and that their thinking was sound because, according to the most brilliant contemporary thinkers, the civilization and culture of a people are fundamentally and closely related to religious concepts. And in Quebec, as in the rest of Canada, for that matter, the basis of our religious beliefs is of Christian or of Jewish-Christian origin.
We would have liked the political leaders of our province to understand the meaning of their mandate and decide to endorse it adequately. But nothing of the sort happened, Mr. Speaker, and I challenge you to find any political leader in Quebec at present, or any of the so-called press, radio or television experts who have the blessing of the political leaders, who have made statements based on Christian ethics or related thereto.
The reason I mention these things, Mr. Speaker, is that the presentation of the budget may have very significant effects in the province of Quebec. And the harm that results on both sides could be prevented or reduced if Christian principles were applied. For instance, who would dare to say: What can Quebec bring to Canada or even to the world? Or: How could the federal government enable the province of Quebec to make a more efficient contribution to her own citizens and to the rest of Canada?
After all, it is Christian charity which bids us to love and to give, not to command and to take.

When we realize the game Russia is playing, anything is possible.

Imaginary enemies will be thrown before French Canada ... and eventually it will be led to put its neck in a noose.
Although, Mr. Speaker, a few well respected and well learned priests are preaching actual separation, it seems to me that the separatist theory and principles are almost diametrically opposed to the Christian concept and the brotherhood of man, and completely opposed to the appeal made by the late Pope John XXIII two years ago, when he called on the Catholics of Europe to work towards the realization of European unity.
I quote from La Presse:
(Translation):
To build gradually the European unity, it is necessary to beat isolation and narrow nationalism. Only hearts and minds united in the same faith and love can result in such a community.
The recent death of Pope John XXIII was a great loss for the world. And I think, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members, regardless of their religious beliefs, will admit that he did a lot to change and improve contemporary thinking. Incidentally as the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) said, I believe I express the views of many when I suggest in all deference that it is about time our country set up a Canadian embassy at the Vatican. John XXIII is the author of two encyclicals Mater et Magistra and Pacem in Terris which are considered by the whole world as the most comprehensive and most searching documents on modern social and political thinking.
Such writings are studied and commented upon everywhere, here and abroad, but unfortunately, their practical consequences do not seem to interest our national or Quebec leaders. Of all the aspects of Quebec's political evolution, very few were related so far, closely or even loosely, to that type of philosophy. To the contrary, we hear today revolutionary principles which run counter to the usual pattern of thought in this country.

Speaking as a physician, I would be tempted to say that a revolutionist is often a peculiar man, I nearly said a peculiar patient.
Very often, he is riddled with feelings of insecurity, or with an inferiority complex, because he has been deeply wounded some time in the past and nurtures, without even knowing it, feelings of revenge and of destruction. Castro and Che Guevera are men of that ilk.
It is unfortunate that such types may be found in Quebec, as well as in the rest of Canada. It may be encouraging to know that they are few in numbers but it should not be forgotten that they have a fighting spirit and that they hold great attraction for the masses.
I expect certain progressive minds to ridicule me and to accuse me of witch hunting but I would like you to know, sir, that I feel in good company since I have the support of people who follow the principles of Christian philosophy.
Naturally, the few remarks I made a moment ago apply neither to the serious-minded and conscientious reporters of the press gallery nor to the responsible philosophers and theologians from Quebec and the whole of Canada who keep constant watch on the situation to increase our national inheritance but who prefer to remain out of the public eye. In my opinion, they deserve our thanks for their great contribution to the Canadian community.
To come back to the budget, Mr. Speaker- although my digression served to emphasize the complexity of the federal-provincial fiscal relations-I can tell you that the people of Quebec were quite surprised to find out that Messrs. Lamontagne, Sauve, Tremblay, Pepin and others failed in their efforts to convince the Minister of Finance of our province's urgent needs.
I should like to take this opportunity to make a bitter reproach to the premier of the province of Quebec, the Hon. Jean Lesage. During the last election campaign, contrary to all the traditions in that respect, he sided officially with the federal Liberal party and he stated that the latter was Quebec's best guarantee of a fair treatment. Now, the present budget bears witness to the fact that Mr. Lesage misinformed the people of our province. Either he knew what the present government held in store for them or he did not know. If he did, he had no right to deceive the public with hopes which now appear to be utopian. If he did not know, he had no more right to mislead them for purely political considerations.


I should also like to point out that Quebec already levies 17 per cent of the personal income and that with just another 8 per cent, it will make the 25 per cent requested.
No matter what difficulties are involved, it is absolutely necessary that a government for the people and by the people agree to give back to the provinces all the privileges guaranteed to them by the B.N.A. Act, as recommended in the Tremblay commission report.
I do not see why it should be necessary for the central government to have all the sources of taxation in order to exercise an influence on the Canadian economy, as said the Minister of Finance.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the Hon. Jean Lesage who, when he was federal minister of northern affairs and national resources stated, as reported in the Quebec paper L'Action of June 7, 1957:
No matter what is said, there is not in Mont-magny a single labour problem which comes under federal jurisdiction.
He seemed to indicate that the question of unemployment was a responsibility for Quebec. And nowadays, he tries to prove that all Quebec misfortunes are caused by the federal government. It would have been better for this man, when he sat in this house, to demand Quebec rights instead of asking for their transfer in Ottawa. Besides, when you consider that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne), the member for Outremont-St. Jean still has his nose in those fiscal matters, you must admit that there is nothing too reassuring for Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words concerning the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. It should be recalled that the inquiry made by the Liberal government in 1955 gave absolutely nothing. At the most, it benumbed the hon. members of that time, who were quite happy because they did not have to voice stronger demands for their compatriots. The government should immediately proceed with it, because, as the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine so rightly said in the house on May 22 last, and the hon. member for Outremont today- French Canadians know where the errors lie and cannot wait for the results of such an inquiry.
I also want to stress that, contrary to certain press reports, the "Gregoire commission" is not a royal commission and that, when I referred to the inefficiency of the so-called commissioner, I meant that, during

an investigation other than on bilingualism, he had proved, without doubt, that he had not succeeded in making great discoveries. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the face of it perhaps the suggestion has some merit, but my opinion is that things of this nature should be settled behind the curtains, behind the Speaker's chair, and not raised as a matter for discussion. Under these circumstances, particularly in view of the fact that I have already apprised the house leader that his suggestion has been very carefully considered by us, for a number of reasons we are of the opinion that we should follow the normal course of proceedings. Wednesday can be protracted with written questions and notices of motion for production of papers; it can also move very quickly if answers are produced speedily without argument. We think that there is no need to extend a debate which has now gone for five days, and it is rather unusual for a government to ask to have a debate extended. We ourselves are not asking for that, yet in fact we may have more to say on the budget debate than people on the other side. But in any case, having considered the matter very, very carefully, we prefer to carry on with the normal order of business.

subtopic: LETTER TO PROVINCES RESPECTING PENSIONS

speechtext:
June 20,1963
The government has placed before parliament a resolution on contributory old age pensions as the first step in implementing a comprehensive Canada-wide pension program. A copy of this resolution is enclosed for your information. As soon as the bill has been presented to parliament, copies will be forwarded to you so that you may be acquainted fully with the details of the Canada pension plan which the government hopes will receive the approval of parliament.
The new plan is designed to overcome shortcomings in existing federal pension provisions. Benefits from this plan, related to previous earnings, combined with the existing flat rate pension, will enable Canadians to retire in reasonable security. Pensioners will be afforded the option of obtaining an adjusted pension from age 65.
The advantages of a comprehensive federal plan of this kind include, of course, the fact that it alone can assure full portability of pensions and can enable earnings-related pensions to be paid on a full scale after a relatively short transition period.
However, implementation of the Canada pension plan will not in itself be sufficient to meet a number of other closely related problems. The provision of benefits for widows below pension age with dependant children, for orphans and for disabled persons are matters of mutual concern for federal and provincial governments. Since the inclusion of these benefits in a federal program would raise jurisdictional questions they are not a part of the proposed Canada pension plan.
While many provincial governments indicated to my predecessor their willingness to have the jurisdictional question clarified, in my opinion this is an area which requires full consultation and discussion between federal and provincial governments, in order that a satisfactory approach can be worked out. Provincial governments will want to know in some detail what the federal government has in mind with regard to such ancillary benefits. The whole question of joint federal-provincial program in the field of old age assistance and disability allowances is also involved. The time required to explore these various possibilities, however, need not
delay immediate steps for the improvement of benefits for our older citizens.
While the benefits under the proposed, new federal plan will be relatively generous, there will continue to be an important place for private pension arrangements. These pension arrangements now afford many industrial workers a considerable measure of protection. However, the growth of such plans has brought to the fore a number of special problems. The absence of vesting of employer contributions interferes with labour mobility. The lack of assurance that contributions are set aside for future retirement, when an employee leaves a firm, tends to weaken the effect of such schemes in making adequate provision for retirement benefits. The solvency of private pension plans also continues to be a concern.
Questions such as these have led several of the provincial governments to give consideration to supervision of private pension plans in order to ensure that certain basic standards are met.
Ontario now has legislation designed to achieve these objectives for private pension plans within its jurisdiction. The federal government's interest in this field relates to federal employees, to employees of companies coming within federal jurisdiction, and to reciprocal arrangements which may be necessary for any interprovincial and federal-provincial aspects of this question. The Canada pension plan which parliament will soon be considering will complement any efforts of this nature to ensure portability and solvency of private pension plans.
It is apparent that these matters are of special concern to our respective governments and 1 would like to suggest that they be the subject of federal-provincial discussions as soon as possible. I would appreciate your letting me know, at your earliest convenience, whether such discussion is acceptable. In the light of this information, I hope shortly to suggest the earliest possible date which seems to be generally convenient for a meeting of ministers.
The development of more equitable programs of social welfare measures both now and in the future is a matter of mutual interest. We hope that the discussions proposed will be a constructive means of achieving common objectives.
Yours sincerely,
